transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-02
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 min
Attendees: Ava M (Redwood AE), Diego C (Redwood SE), Rina P (Kestrel Platform), Omar H (Kestrel ML Infra), Priya S (Product)

Summary:
Quick kickoff to scope the POC for Kestrel's contextual search product. Main goals: agree success criteria (latency, cost, quality), capture workload sizing and token distributions, define benchmark plan and timeline, and propose reserved GPU + burst/fallback strategy for the POC.

Topics:
- POC success criteria and SLAs
- Traffic profile and sizing (steady qps, burst characteristics, tokens)
- Reserved GPU sizing and autoscale windows
- Burst strategy and fallback policies (queueing, degrade to smaller model, hosted fallback)
- Security constraints (VPC, KMS, data retention)
- Next steps and owners

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros then we'll jump into what you want to prove in this POC.
[00:12] Rina (Kestrel): Hi all — Rina here. We're the platform team, supporting the search product. Omar's our infra lead, Priya is the PM.
[00:18] Omar: Hi, thanks. We mainly need to see predictable cost and latency, and make sure we can integrate with our VPC and KMS.
[00:25] Diego (Redwood): Great. I'll start with a one-slide run-through of how we typically size reserved + burst for 1–3 week POCs, then we can map to your traffic.

[00:34] Diego: High level — for POCs we recommend a baseline reserved pool sized for steady-state QPS, plus a burst pool to absorb peak spikes. We also set a fallback policy so that if capacity is exhausted we either queue or route to a lower-cost hosted model.
[00:48] Priya: Can you explain what you mean by "lower-cost hosted model" — is that Redwood hosted API?
[00:53] Diego: Yeah, that's the hosted endpoint — same API semantics, different deployment. It's typically a smaller model or lower concurrency path. It's used as a graceful degradation path to avoid 5xx errors during extreme spikes.

[01:05] Rina: Our typical steady is around 60 requests per second, but we have frequent bursts up to 420 rps during batch ingest windows; burst lasts 4–7 minutes. Token sizes vary a lot — median input ~90 tokens, generation ~60 tokens but some longer.
[01:23] Omar: Also, some requests are long-context queries where we attach embeddings and prior-turn KV cache; peak memory can be a constraint.

[01:33] Diego: That's helpful — so for rough math, assuming avg generation 60 tokens and model throughput like a 13B quantized variant, a single A100-style worker gives X tokens/sec. For safety in POC we usually present three variants: conservative (reserve capacity for steady plus 25% buffer), balanced (steady + 100% headroom), and aggressive (steady + 300% burst).
[01:55] Ava: We'll tailor those to your cost target and SLA. What are your success criteria? Latency p95, cost per 1k requests, and no >1% error rate?

[02:05] Priya: Priority order: 1) p95 latency under 350 ms for interactive flows, 2) max cost per 1k under $5 (POC target), 3) model output hang or quality within existing baseline (we'll share eval prompts).
[02:19] Diego: Ok noted. For p95 350ms, depending on sequence length and model, you'll likely need reserved concurrency to avoid queueing latency.

[02:28] Rina: How do you actually implement bursting? Do you spin up new reserved machines or use preemptible capacity?
[02:33] Diego: For Redwood Dedicated POC we configure a reserved pool (customer-dedicated) and allow a configurable burst pool. Burst can be either warm burst (kept on hot but billed differently) or cold burst (spin-up from shared capacity). Warm burst gives lowest latency but costs more. Cold burst can introduce upward latency during spin-up.

[02:50] Omar: Spin-up times kill user experience if they happen in the middle of a session. Is queueing acceptable?
[02:55] Ava: We recommend a hybrid approach — short spikes get absorbed by warm burst or queued for up to 2–3s, beyond that route to hosted fallback model with slightly lower quality. We can also pre-warm based on schedule (you mentioned daily ingest windows).

[03:11] Priya: We can predict some windows — nightly batch and morning ramp. But sometimes marketing runs unexpected campaigns.
[03:18] Diego: For unpredictable spikes, an automatic fallback policy helps: 1) queue for up to X seconds, 2) if queue exceeded switch to hosted smaller model, 3) surface an SLA warning in your dashboard and notify via webhook.

[03:32] Rina: About KV cache — in our tests we saw KV cache eviction thrash under high concurrency. Any recommendations?
[03:39] Diego: We can tune KV cache shard size and memory allocation per instance; the runtime exposes cache hit metrics. For POC we'll include a KV cache eviction metric in the benchmark so we can see when quality degrades due to misses.

[03:50] Priya: Benchmarks — what will you run?
[03:53] Diego: We'll run a 2-hour steady-state at your 95th percentile steady load and a set of synthetic bursts: 5-minute ramp to 4x steady, 10-minute spike to 6–7x, and 1-minute microbursts to 10x. We'll exercise different token distributions (short, medium, long). We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latency, token SRT, GPU utilization, and cost estimate.

[04:16] Omar: We need to run benchmarks inside our VPC — can you support VPC peering and KMS?
[04:21] Ava: Yes — for the Private deployment we do VPC peering and support customer KMS with HSM-backed keys. We'll need a peering CIDR and an IAM/service account. Diego will send the checklist.

[04:33] Rina: For the POC size, what numbers are you thinking?
[04:36] Diego: Based on 60 rps steady and observed bursts, a balanced starting point is: reserve 8 GPU workers sized for the model variant (13B quant), warm burst pool of 6 extra workers, and cold burst cap of 10 (on shared infra). That gives steady capacity for 60 rps with headroom and can hit 420 rps with queued+fallback tolerances. Conservative would be 4 reserved + 3 warm burst; aggressive 12 reserved + 12 warm burst.

[05:02] Priya: Can you provide cost estimates for each variant?
[05:05] Ava: Yes, Diego will produce a 3-scenario cost sheet — we’ll include token cost, instance-hour cost, and an estimate for warm burst billing.

[05:12] Omar: What's the fallback model quality delta? How much worse is the smaller hosted model?
[05:17] Diego: Typically a smaller 6–7B model will have slightly lower factuality in long-context queries. For many search/rerank use cases it still passes quality gates. We'll run the eval prompts you provide. Also we can enable automatic prompt routing — keep semantic-critical requests on reserved path and route low-criticality background requests to hosted.

[05:34] Rina: Timeline for POC — we want a 3-week engagement where week 0 is setup, week 1 baseline + quick perf, week 2 parameter tuning and extended run, week 3 decision. Is that realistic?
[05:44] Ava: Yes, that matches our common POC cadence. Setup includes peering, dataset, and a short warm-up run. We'll aim to start benchmarks by week 1 and have results for week 2 tuning.

[05:53] Priya: How do rollouts work — if POC is successful how do we migrate to dedicated prod?
[05:58] Diego: You can pin model versions and rollout strategies in the console. We support gradual canaries and blue-green. The POC reserved pool can be converted to production reserved capacity with an SLA uplift and contract.

[06:08] Omar: Security — we need SOC2 + ISO docs and audit logs for each request.
[06:13] Ava: We'll send SOC2 and ISO27001 certs, and you can turn on request-level audit logs. Logs can be pushed to your logging infra or kept in Redwood with retention policies.

[06:23] Rina: One technical deep-dive — what about model quantization and its effect on latency variability?
[06:28] Diego: Quantization reduces memory and increases throughput but can add variance for long-sequence attention patterns. For POC we'll test a quantized 13B and, if needed, a 16-bit variant to measure differences. We'll capture per-token latency distribution.

[06:40] Priya: Are there any real risks that would make this POC infeasible?
[06:44] Diego: Biggest risks: inability to peer VPC in time, or token distribution much longer than estimated which requires different instance types. We mitigate by running initial synthetic tests and smoothing expectations.

[06:55] Rina: For the success criteria doc you mentioned — include error budget thresholds and what constitutes a pass/fail?
[06:59] Ava: Yes — we'll propose pass if p95 <= 350ms for interactive flows, error rate <= 1%, and cost delta <= 20% of your target. We'll also include quality-eval pass thresholds based on the prompts you provide.

[07:12] Omar: On observability — can we get token-level cost and per-route dashboards?
[07:17] Diego: Yes, Console has token-level breakdowns, per-model latency heatmaps, and traces. We will attach synthetic traces for the benchmark so you can rule out hotspots.

[07:25] Priya: Any callbacks we'll need to configure?
[07:27] Ava: We'll set up a webhook for capacity alerts and another for benchmark completion. Diego: and a health check endpoint so your infra can detect degraded throughput.

[07:36] Rina: Ok, let's recap the concrete asks from Kestrel: provide anonymized traffic profile, share evaluation prompts, and confirm PII constraints for dataset.
[07:45] Priya: We'll get those over — PII is allowed in hashed/anonymized form; we need to sign an NDA addendum?
[07:52] Ava: We can attach a data processing addendum. I'll follow up with legal.

[08:00] Diego: I'll summarize the proposed sizing options in a spreadsheet — conservative/balanced/aggressive — with estimated p95 and cost. We'll also include three benchmark scenarios and the exact scripts.

[08:10] Omar: About routing policy — can we set rules like "if request includes header X then always go to reserved pool"?
[08:15] Diego: Absolutely — route-by-header or route-by-token or by route name is supported. That's a good way to protect high-importance requests.

[08:23] Priya: What about rate limiting and quota — we want to avoid noisy neighbors on shared infra.
[08:28] Ava: Redwoods console has per-route rate limiting; for POC we'll recommend per-API-key quotas and burst windows. Also reserved pool isolates you from shared usage.

[08:38] Rina: For cost modelling — will you provide a measured cost after the benchmark so we can reconcile with our finance team?
[08:43] Diego: Yes — each benchmark run will output an invoice-style breakdown (instance-hrs, token cost, warm-burst time).

[08:50] Priya: Any blockers we should know about?
[08:53] Rina: We need the peering schedule — we can only do peering maintenance windows on Sundays.
[08:58] Ava: We'll accommodate that.

[09:02] Diego: Ok. Final quick questions — do you expect multi-region?
[09:06] Rina: Not initially. We'll run in us-west and maybe later add eu-west.

[09:10] Diego: Noted. We'll size for us-west deploys only.

[09:14] Priya: Anything else on fallback semantics? Do you support partial response fallback (like returning cached partial result and continuing generation)?
[09:22] Diego: We have streaming partial responses and you can configure timeouts; if the backend can't finish we can return a partial token stream and a status code indicating degraded result. We'll include streams in the benchmark.

[09:34] Rina: Sounds good. Let's confirm the timeline: Ava to send docs by EOW, Diego to send benchmark and sizing by next Tues, Kestrel to provide traffic and prompts by Fri, week of 8/9 do live runs.

[09:47] Ava: Correct — I'll include the NDA addendum and peering checklist in the follow-up.

[09:55] Priya: Great, thanks everyone.
[09:57] Omar: Thanks.
[09:59] Diego: Thanks — we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the benchmark window.

[10:04] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: some terms transcribed imperfectly — e.g., "K V cash" for KV cache, "S L A" split, model names generalized. There are short crosstalk moments and filler words preserved.

POC deliverables (from call):
- Sizing spreadsheet: conservative/balanced/aggressive with cost estimates and expected p95
- Benchmark harness: scripts for steady + burst + microburst scenarios
- Success criteria doc (latency, cost, quality thresholds)
- VPC peering and KMS checklist
- Schedule for live benchmark week of 2027-08-09

Benchmark quick numbers (ballpark supplied on call):
- Steady: 60 rps, median input 90 tokens, gen 60 tokens
- Burst targets: 4x for 5–7m, 7x for 10m, 10x microbursts 30–60s
- Suggested balanced reserve: 8 GPUs + 6 warm-burst workers; conservative: 4 GPUs + 3 warm; aggressive: 12 + 12
- Latency target: p95 <= 350ms for interactive; error rate <1%

End of transcript.
